# Exact-dimension Brunn-Minkowski for finite mixed fibers

Let d>=1,n>=0, put Lambda=Z^n x R^d, and write

mu(E)=sum_{z in Z^n} vol_d(E_z)

for compact subsets E of Lambda. Such a set has finitely many nonempty compact fibers, so its mixed volume is finite. Minkowski sums of two such compact sets are again compact subsets of Lambda, with finitely many nonempty fibers. Their fiber measures are ordinary Lebesgue measures.

## Theorem 1: unrestricted sum inequality

For nonempty compact A,B subset Lambda,

mu(A+B) >= (mu(A)^{1/d}+mu(B)^{1/d})^d.

The nonempty hypothesis is necessary: if A is empty and mu(B)>0, the displayed inequality fails.

Proof for positive total volumes. Put A0=mu(A)>0 and B0=mu(B)>0. Ignore zero-volume fibers for the moment. List the positive-volume fibers of A at z_1,...,z_m and of B at w_1,...,w_k, with respective volumes a_i,b_j.

If n>=1, choose a linear functional ell on R^n that takes distinct values at distinct points of the finite union of these two index sets. Such a functional exists because the forbidden choices lie in finitely many proper linear hyperplanes. Order both lists increasingly by ell. When n=0 there is just one index in each list, and the assertion is ordinary Brunn-Minkowski, so assume n>=1 below.

Partition [0,1) into consecutive half-open intervals I_i of lengths a_i/A0, in this order, and into consecutive half-open intervals J_j of lengths b_j/B0. Let

q_ij=length(I_i intersect J_j).

Then q_ij>=0, sum_{i,j}q_ij=1, and

q_ij<=a_i/A0, q_ij<=b_j/B0.

The pairs (i,j) with q_ij>0 form a chain in the coordinatewise order. Indeed, as a parameter t moves through [0,1), the unique indices satisfying t in I_i and t in J_j never decrease. Each pair occurs on one interval. After ordering these positive cells by t, every transition increases at least one index and decreases neither.

Consequently all selected sum indices z_i+w_j are distinct: their ell values strictly increase at each transition. For each selected pair, the fiber (A+B)_{z_i+w_j} contains A_{z_i}+B_{w_j}. Classical Brunn-Minkowski gives

vol_d((A+B)_{z_i+w_j})
>= (a_i^{1/d}+b_j^{1/d})^d
>= q_ij (A0^{1/d}+B0^{1/d})^d.

The last step follows from a_i>=q_ij A0 and b_j>=q_ij B0. Summing over the distinct selected fibers, and using sum q_ij=1, proves the theorem. Other pairs may contribute to the same fibers, but they were not counted separately. Zero-volume fibers omitted from the coupling can only add points and volume to A+B, so omitting them is legitimate.

Zero-volume cases. If both totals vanish, the claimed lower bound is zero. If A0=0 and B0>0, choose a point a in nonempty A. Then a+B is a subset of A+B and has mixed volume B0: its integer indices are translated bijectively and its continuous fibers are translated isometrically. Thus mu(A+B)>=B0, the required bound. The other case is symmetric.

## Corollary 2: same-parity midpoint inequality

If A and B are nonempty compact subsets supported over the same coset p+2Z^n, then (A+B)/2 is a compact subset of Lambda and

mu((A+B)/2)
>= [ (mu(A)^{1/d}+mu(B)^{1/d})/2 ]^d.

Indeed A+B has only even integer indices. Dividing both coordinate groups by two sends its integer-index set bijectively to integer indices and scales each continuous fiber volume by 2^{-d}. Therefore mu((A+B)/2)=2^{-d}mu(A+B), and Theorem 1 applies. This tracks the measure transformation exactly; no factor 2^{-n} occurs in this scaling because the integer fibers carry counting measure.

## Lemma 3: stronger monotone-path lower bounds

List any finite nonempty fibers of A and B in increasing order under the same generic functional ell; zero-volume nonempty fibers may be included. For every full monotone grid path P from (1,1) to (m,k), using steps (1,0) or (0,1),

mu(A+B) >= sum_{(i,j) in P} (a_i^{1/d}+b_j^{1/d})^d.

Every successive path step strictly increases ell(z_i+w_j), so all sum indices along the path are distinct. Apply ordinary Brunn-Minkowski separately at those fibers and add. The same-parity midpoint version divides the right side by 2^d.

This path inequality is often strictly stronger than Theorem 1. It does not rely on a coupling and is a directly computable finite lower bound.

## Corollary 4: quantitative parity expansion inside a convex body

Let C be compact convex, and let A be a nonempty compact subset of C supported over one parity coset. Order its nonempty fiber indices z_1,...,z_m by a generic functional, and let their volumes be a_1,...,a_m, allowing zero volumes. Then

mu(C intersect Lambda)
>= mu((A+A)/2)
>= sum_{i=1}^m a_i
   + sum_{i=1}^{m-1} [ (a_i^{1/d}+a_{i+1}^{1/d})/2 ]^d.

Convexity puts (A+A)/2 inside C, and parity makes all its integer coordinates integral. In Lemma 3 use the path

(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(2,3),...,(m-1,m),(m,m).

Its diagonal cells yield the sum of original fiber volumes, and its off-diagonal cells yield the displayed midpoint contributions. The off-diagonal midpoint indices lie strictly between consecutive ordered source indices under ell. They therefore coincide with neither an indexed source fiber nor another selected midpoint, so no mass is counted twice.

## Corollary 5: strictness when a set has multiple fibers

If mu(A),mu(B)>0 and at least one of A,B has more than one nonempty fiber, then the inequality in Theorem 1 is strict.

For positive-volume fibers, equality in the coupling proof's inequality for a cell q_ij>0 requires both a_i=q_ij A0 and b_j=q_ij B0, because the function (s^{1/d}+t^{1/d})^d is strictly increasing in each positive argument. Thus each row and each column can meet only one positive cell. If all cells have equality, the two normalized interval partitions coincide, giving matched diagonal cells. If there is more than one such cell, insert the cell between the first and second matched diagonal cells. Its sum index lies strictly between the first two diagonal sum indices and is distinct from all of them; its Minkowski-sum fiber has positive volume. This adds a strictly positive amount beyond the coupling bound. If any coupling cell inequality is strict, strictness already follows directly.

Thus equality can only occur when each set has one positive-volume fiber. If either then has an additional nonempty zero-volume fiber, adding that fiber to the other set's positive-volume fiber produces a distinct sum fiber of positive volume (fix a point in the zero-volume fiber). This again forces strictness. Hence equality requires each set to have exactly one nonempty fiber. The remaining equality question is precisely the ordinary continuous Brunn-Minkowski equality question for those two fibers.

## Boundary of applicability

These theorems do not assert that a parity component is convex, that its midpoint sum stays in the same parity component, or that the sum of midpoint volumes from different parity components is disjoint. In general it is not disjoint. In Corollary 4 the midpoint sum stays in the whole convex mixed set, which is exactly the property used. No centerpoint conclusion or existence of a favorable parity component follows automatically.
